translations.text: Discourse of Saint Basil on drunkards, which he delivered one day after the breaking of the fast.
The deeds of this past evening have moved me to speak. Yet the fruitlessness of my former labors in turn restrains my impulse,
for a farmer too, when what he has sown once does not yield fruit, is reluctant to sow a second time on the same ground.
For if, after so many teachings that we gave during the past season of the year, when we did not cease entreating you, and again during these seven weeks of the fast,
night and day, I did not cease testifying to you the gospel of the grace of God, and no benefit came of all this, with what hope then should I teach you today?
O how many nights you kept vigil in vain, how many days you gathered in vain, if indeed it was only in vain,
for whoever has come to make progress in good deeds and afterward turns back again to his former habits,
not only loses the reward of what he has labored for, but also becomes deserving of a greater judgment,
for he has seen the taste of the good words of God and has been made worthy of the spiritual mysteries, and then he has disregarded all of it for the sake of a small desire.
"For the ignorant one is worthy of pardon, but the mighty will be mightily tormented."
One night and one assault of the devil has destroyed all that labor and made it vanish. How then can I be eager to speak now?
And know that I would have kept silent, if I had not been afraid because of what happened to the prophet Jeremiah,
who did not wish to speak to that rebellious people, and therefore there came upon him, as he himself says, that:
a fire came to be in his loins, and he was consumed on every side and could not endure it.
But now wicked women have forgotten the fear of God and have despised the eternal fire on such a day as this,
when, for the remembrance of the resurrection, they ought to have sat in their own houses and called to mind that day when the heavens will be opened and the Judge will appear from heaven:
and the trumpets of God, and the resurrection of the dead, and the righteous judgment, and the repayment of each according to his deeds.
Instead of practicing such things, and instead of purifying their hearts of evil thoughts and wiping away their sins with tears, and instead of preparing
to meet Christ on that great day of his appearing, they cast off the yoke of service to Christ and tore from their heads the veils of honor,
they disregarded God and disregarded his angels, and became shameless before the face of men:
and they let down their hair, trailed their garments, and danced with their feet, with a filthy eye,
with shameless laughter they were stirred to dancing and frenzy, and they defiled the hearts of the young men, and before those churches
which are outside the city they set up dancers, and they made those holy places the place of their own abomination.
They defiled the air with their harlots' voices and defiled the ground with their unclean feet, with which they performed that dance.
And they arranged a multitude of foolish young men around them as spectators; they became maddened harlots and left no limit to their frenzy.
How could I keep silent about all this? Or how could I lament it as it deserves?
Wine has lured upon us this kind of shipwreck of souls: wine, which God gave as a comfort for the weakness of the wise, but which has now become an instrument of sin for those fools.
Drunkenness: that voluntary demon-possession, a demon procured by human beings, which enters the soul through the desires;

drunkenness: mother of wickedness, opponent of virtue. It makes the brave man fearful, it makes the honorable man shameless, it makes the pure man foul; it does not know righteousness, it destroys wisdom.
For just as water fights against fire, so drunkenness extinguishes wisdom.
For this reason I too shrink from speaking about drunkenness, not as though it were some small and contemptible evil, but because I see no benefit coming from the speech.
For if the drunkard is senseless and darkened, the teacher counsels that man who cannot hear in vain.
To whom, then, should our speech be addressed, since the one who needs teaching does not listen to these words?
And the one who is sober in mind does not need teaching, for he is pure of that passion.
What then shall I do, even though the speech is useless? Yet silence is impossible. What then shall I do? Shall I neglect this speech?
But neglect is dangerous. Or shall I say something about drunkards? We would be groaning into dead ears.
Yet just as, when an incurable, deadly disease falls upon cattle, their healers protect and guard the healthy ones beforehand with medicines,
but do not go near those seized by the disease, so for us too this speech has a benefit in half measure,
for although it may in no way profit those seized by that passion, yet those who have not yet fallen into it may perhaps take care.
By what are you set apart from the beasts, O man? Is it not by that gift of reason which you have received from the Creator? Have you been made ruler and lord of all the world?
So now, whoever thus drives his wisdom mad through drunkenness, "he has imitated the senseless beasts and become like them."
But I call drunkards even more senseless and more beastly than the beasts, for all four-footed animals and wild beasts have an appointed time for mating and for bearing young,
whereas those seized by drunkenness fill the nature of the body with an external heat, and at every time go after those defiled deeds.
And this is not the only sign of their bestiality, but the altered perception of their senses also makes them worse than any beast,
for what sheep or ox is so deaf, so poor of sight and so senseless as a drunkard?
Do they not often fail to recognize their own people, and take strangers for their own?
Do they not often leap over shadows, as if over ditches and as if over waters?
Their ears are full of roaring and hissing, as if from a turbulent sea, and they think that the earth stands tilted upward and that the mountains are running around them.
These people at times laugh without restraint and at times weep without ceasing, and at times are arrogant and insolent and fearless, and then fearful and trembling.
Their sleep is heavy, a kind of suffocation, and truly close to death; and again their waking is more senseless than sleep, for their whole life is a dream.
Those who often have no clothing, nor anything they might eat the next day,
sit as kings and act as commanders of generals in their drunkenness, and they build cities and distribute riches.
With such fantasies and delusion does wine fill their hearts.
But others in turn are sunk by a passion of the opposite kind: they become despairing and sorrowful, weeping and fearful.
The one same wine enters each of these bodies and produces passions of various kinds: for in some it makes boil
the blood and increases it, and so makes them joyful and radiant; while others, by its great heaviness, it weighs down, and it oppresses and lowers the blood, and in this way makes them sad.
And why is there any need to enumerate their other passions?
The fury of their mind, their quick anger, their fault-finding, the bitterness of their soul, how they are stubborn over nothing,
their shouting and the disorder of their voice, their excessive tumult, their easy inclination toward every delusion?
And drunkenness becomes, like a spring, the source of defiling desires, and the [?] of fornication enters along with the abundance of wine,
and the defilement of drunkards puts in the shade all the frenzy of beasts toward their females, for beasts know the boundaries of nature,
but drunkards seek womanhood among men and manhood among women.
It is neither good nor possible to tell in words all the evils of drunkenness.

The diseases of pestilential heat come among people over a length of time, when little by little the disease of the air enters into their bodies, but the diseases that come from wine arrive in an instant.
For in this way, along with the ruin and defilement of the soul, the health of the flesh is also taken away and their appearance is changed,
not only because they are so eager for filthy acts, but because their very body is sick and has no natural strength:
their eyes are livid [?], their face far from its natural color, their breath constricted, their tongue impaired, their voice disordered, and their feet hasty,
stumbling like those of little children, and the discharges of their excess come out of their own accord, as if flowing from lifeless things.
They are pitiable in their pleasure, more pitiable than those tossed about at sea,
upon whom wave after wave comes, one upon another, and does not let them lift their heads; just so the souls of these men are sunk in the waves of wine.
And then, just as ships, when they come near to sinking, throw off their cargo, so too these men,
when they can no longer bear that evil heaviness, begin to vomit and to be loathsome, and thus with difficulty they are rid of that heaviness.
So much more pitiable are they than those tossed about at sea, for the cause of those men's distress was the violence of the winds and the waves of the sea,
but these men of their own free will bring upon their own heads the storm of drunkenness.
A demoniac is to be pitied, but the drunkard, who is engaged in the very deeds of a demoniac, is not worthy of mercy, for he has made himself possessed of his own will.
Those who seek remedies for drunkenness do so not in order to suffer no harm from wine, but in order not to have to stop drinking.
For in their eyes the day is short and contemptible, and even the longest of the winter nights is short for drinking.
And there is no end to this evil, for wine itself makes more room for itself.
For it is no relief for their weakness, but rather a summons to further drinking,
when it burns the drunkards and lures them to desire more, and they have an unending craving for drink and wish to have an even greater craving.
And the opposite of what they want happens to them, for through immoderate drinking they destroy their own senses.
For just as excessive brightness darkens the eyes, and just as those stunned by a loud and harsh noise can no longer hear because of the harshness of that noise,
so these people do not realize that, through their excessive love of taste, they have ruined their taste for drink.
For the wine is tasteless and watery in their mouths, even if it is undiluted, and it is lukewarm in their mouths, even if it is like ice
or chilled with snow, for it cannot quench the flame that burns within them because of the wine.
See: "Who has woe? Who has tumult? Whose are the ruinations? Whose are the needless bruises and the nausea of the heart?
Whose eyes are livid? Is it not those who have given themselves over to drinking wine and who watch for where drinking is going on?"
"Woe" is a word of mourning, and drunkards are worthy of mourning, for they will not inherit the kingdom of heaven.
And "tumult" is the disturbance that wine produces in the mind;
and "nausea of the heart" refers to the bitter tastes that arise in the heart when the excessive wine dissolves there.
For their hands are bound and their feet are fettered by the gout that comes from drunkenness, and even before this, at the very time of drinking, the behavior of madmen comes upon them.
For when the passages of the temples are filled with the smoke that wine sends up to them with its vapor,
then the head is seized by immeasurable pains and cannot stand upright on the shoulders, but lolls from side to side on the neck.
And further, the many "ruinations" are their useless and quarrelsome schemes, and the "needless bruises" are those that come upon them,
who because of drunkenness cannot stand upright, but fall in every direction and are bruised for nothing.
But who will tell all this to those stricken by wine? For they are deaf and sleepy, they nod [?], a fog is spread over them, and they are tossed about as if on waves.
For this reason they do not hear the teaching of the teachers, who cry out to them from every side:
"Do not get drunk with wine, in which there is filthiness," and again: "Wine-bibbing is evil and drunkenness is insulting."
And they disobey these words, but they themselves reap the fruit of drunkenness, for the body becomes swollen, the eyes moist, and the mouth dry and parched.
For just as riverbeds, so long as streams flow through them, are reckoned full, and when that water passes away they are left dry,
so too is the mouth of drunkards: so long as wine stands in it, it is full and moist, but when a little time passes,
it becomes dry and parched; and when the practice of drunkenness is prolonged in this way, all moisture dries out of it entirely.
For what human body could acquire such strength as to bear those evils of drunkenness?
For a body that is always burning and always soaked with wine, what means could keep it from being weak and corrupted?

This is how tremblings and diseases arise: the passage of their breathing is narrowed by the heat of the wine, and the sinews go slack from being stretched out, and thus trembling comes upon the body.
Why then, O man, do you bring upon your own head the curse that was given to Cain, of going about and living in trembling?
So that you likewise may tremble from the evils of wine all your days?
For when the body does not have its natural firmness, it therefore sways about and trembles.
How long will there be wine, how long will there be this drunkenness of yours, O wretched one? For do you not see what is coming upon you? For you are becoming mud instead of a man,
you who have been so wholly mixed with wine, and rot along with it every day in that drunkenness of yours, and stink of rotten, foul-smelling wine, like a useless vessel.
Therefore Isaiah laments over such people, saying: "Woe to those who rise at dawn and pursue strong drink, who stay at it until evening,
for that wine has burned them up; for with harps [?] and pipes they drink that wine, and they do not look to the works of the Lord, and they do not contemplate the work of his hands."
Now everything capable of making one drunk is called strong drink by the Jews.
So then, those who at dawn seek only drinking and drunkenness, and where there will be drinking parties and purchases of wine, and who bring one another along
to drink in shares, and spend all the care of the soul on such things: over such people the prophet mourns.
For they have not left themselves a single hour for seeing the wonders of God, and their eyes have no leisure to look up to heaven and contemplate its beauties and to understand all the good things
that are among created things, so that from the order of all these they might perceive the Creator.
Instead, immediately at the coming of day, as soon as it dawns, they adorn the places of their drinking with rugs [?] and with courts [?] of every kind and of many colors.
And all their effort goes into preparing the drinking vessels: they prepare coolers and cups and chalices, as if for a market.
They arrange them in this way so that the variety and unbroken array [?] of the vessels may steal satiety away from them and they may be able to drink more,
and again, so that changing from one drinking vessel to another may pass a great deal of time in the drinking.

Over all this there are masters of the table and chief cupbearers and chiefs of the wine cellar, and thus order has been devised within that disorder, and management within that unmanageable business.
For just as the glory and honor of the rulers of this world grow through their servants, so also to drunkenness,
as to some queen, they bring their service all around her, and they cover her loathsomeness with excessive honor.
And they place crowns and flowers on her head, and they perfume her with fragrances and incense.
And thus these many entertainments give those lost men a longer stay in the evil.
Then, as the drinking is prolonged, they begin to compete, contending and striving for superiority, those who love to outdo one another in drunkenness.
And the one who gives the prize for their zeal is the devil, and the prize of that victory is sin.
For whoever takes the most and pours that unwatered wine into his belly carries off the victory over the others.
Truly, "their glory is in their shame," for they contend with one another but harm themselves.
What word could reach the foulness of their deeds?
Everything is full of brutishness, everything of evil; the defeated are drunk, the victors are drunk as well, and the servants laugh.
The hand has grown too weak to hold the cups, the mouth takes in no more, the belly is bursting, and still the evil does not abate.
The wretched body is loosened from its natural strength, falls about on every side, and cannot bear the measureless evil.
O pitiable thing in the eyes of Christians! When a man young in age, strong in body,
distinguished in the ranks of the soldiery, is brought home dragged along, because he is unable to stand up and walk on his own feet.
A man who ought to be terrifying for fighters to behold becomes a cause of laughter for children
going about the streets; he is wounded without a sword, slain without a fighter, fettered without iron.
An armed man, in the flower of youth, is made captive by wine and lies ready before his enemies for whatever they wish to befall him.
Drunkenness is the overthrower of the mind, the corrupter of the soul, an untimely old age, a likeness of the dead, similar to an idol; for what else are drunkards but idols of the pagans?
"They have mouths and cannot speak, they have eyes and do not see, they have ears and do not hear"; their hands are loosened, their feet are dead.
Alas, who is it that has done all this evil to us? Who is the cause of these things? Who is it that has handed us the potion of this madness to drink?
O man, have you turned your banquet and your drinking into a battle? For they lead those stalwart young men out of there held up by the hand, like men wounded in battle.
You have killed the vigor of youth with wine: you invite him to supper as a friend, but you send him away as a dead man, for with wine you have destroyed his life.
What am I to say about such people? For when one would suppose that they have had their fill of wine, only then do they begin to drink, and they drink
like cattle, as from a flowing spring, which in equal measure makes the eyes of those drinking spring up [?].
For when their drinking has been prolonged, there comes in among them some stalwart, vigorous young man, who shifts his shoulders about and is not yet drunk, and a large cup is given to him,
filled with chilled wine, and he began to drink, and through those crooked passages he filled his belly with drunkenness, on a level with the others,
so that in this way the measure of that measurelessness might be equal, so that in this way they might all commit that filth alike, and not one be greater or lesser than the others in drunkenness.
For they would share out those great drinking-tubes [?], and each would drink insatiably, as if from a lake, like cattle. He wanted to drink as much as could be found.
Wretched man, look down into that pitiable belly of yours; consider the capacity of the vessel into which so much wine goes down, for it is not even a span in breadth.
Do not look to the wine vessels, to when they will be emptied, but consider your belly, how soon it is filled.
For this reason, "Woe to those who rise at dawn and pursue strong drink and remain at it until evening,
for they have not a single hour to see the works of the Lord or to consider the creation of his hands."
And for this reason "the wine has burned them," for the heat that settles in the flesh from wine becomes fuel for the fiery arrows of the enemy.
And wine lowers and darkens the mind, but stirs up and multiplies the passions and desires.
For what unbroken colt runs so wildly and throws the one sitting on it, or what storm-beaten ship,
having neither pilot nor sailors, is so far astray as a drunken man?
Through such evils as these, men and women together drew up singers and gave their souls over to the demon of drunkenness, and so they shot at one another with the arrow of the passions.
On both sides there was disorderly laughter, filthy songs, and the postures of harlotry, which called them on to defilement.
Do you laugh and rejoice with that evil joy, you who ought to weep and groan for your sins?
Do you recite songs, which lead the way to fornication, in place of the psalms and hymns you have learned?
Do you dance with your feet, and leap, and thrash about, and caper in disorder, you who ought to entreat the Lord on bended knee?
For whom should I mourn first? For the unmarried virgins, or for those who are under the yoke of marriage?
For the former came back no longer having their virginity, and the latter no longer having their former purity, even if from a fall in the flesh
some escaped; yet in mind they were undoubtedly defiled. I say the same also of the men, that:
if "whoever looks at a woman with desire has committed adultery," and if thus a mere chance conversation and desire in thought are so harmful and incur such a judgment,
what then is to become of those who deliberately go out to see and observe such doings and to look at women
who commit obscenities, who are drunk, who perform with that evil acting, and who utter those strains and tunes of fornication,
of whom not the sight but merely the sound of the voice is enough to defile the heart of those stricken with passion?
What will you say to all this, you who go to see them, or who make them sing and dance before you, and through such sights gather to yourselves a countless multitude of passions?
Or is it not evident that you are deliberately eager for this deed, and so become liable to the judgment of adulterers according to the Lord's decree?
Or how will Pentecost receive you, you who have thus made its fulfillment worthless?
For Pentecost has as its work the manifest coming of the Holy Spirit,
but you hasten ahead of it and settle that unclean spirit within yourself, and you become a temple of idols instead of being a temple of God through the indwelling of the Holy Spirit in you.
And you receive the curse of the prophet, who says: "I will turn their feasts into mourning."
Or how are you masters of your slaves, you who have thus been enslaved to lusts?
Or how will you teach your children, you whose own life is untaught and disorderly? What then shall I do?
Shall I leave you with these words? But I fear that the disobedient one may become worse and the contrite one may fall into despair.
Rather, let me show you a medicine that has the power to heal great sins, that is: let fasting heal your drunkenness, and psalm-singing those defiled songs;
let tears be the medicine for laughter; instead of dancing, bend your knees to God; instead of clapping your hands, beat your breast;
instead of that finery of clothing, clothe yourselves in humility. Above all this, let almsgiving redeem you from sin,
for "a man's ransom is his own wealth." Hire many who are afflicted to join you in prayer, that perhaps that evil deed may be forgiven you.

For when "the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play" — and their play was idolatry — then the Levites armed their hands against their brothers, and thus were made perfect in the priesthood.
So likewise you too who are God-fearing, who have now been grieved at the foulness of those evil deeds, this I say to you:
if you see them repenting of the wickedness of their deeds, be compassionate toward them as toward your own weakened members.
But if you see them scorning this distress of ours on their behalf,
"Go out from among them and separate yourselves from them, and touch nothing unclean," so that in this way they too may be ashamed and come to recognize their own evil.
And you will receive the reward of the zeal of Phinehas through the righteous judgments of God and of our Savior Jesus Christ,
to whom belong glory and might now and always and forever and ever, amen.
